title: Nothing on our own
hook: on our own we can do nothing; all happens in His color (Sukhmani 15)

segments.voice: Yesterday, he knows your pain, and your line: he knows. Did you let someone know you saw what they were carrying? Today the fifteenth ashtpadi turns to everything we do, and gives it a color. Day four hundred ninety-six.

In old Punjab, cloth was dyed by hand. You'd soak plain white cotton in a vat, and when you lifted it out, it had become saffron, or indigo, or deep red. Here's the thing about a good dye: it doesn't sit on top of the cloth like paint. It goes into every thread. You can't scrape it off. The cloth is still cloth, but now every part of it carries the color. Gurbani loves that picture, and returns to it again and again. Today it's the way into a hard teaching: nothing on our own.
screen: `WHITE COTTON IN A VAT.` → `SAFFRON, INDIGO, DEEP RED.` → `THE COLOR GOES INTO EVERY THREAD.`

segments.voice: A few days ago, in the eleventh ashtpadi, Sukhmani called God the doer of all. The fifteenth comes back to that thought from a different side. Its message, in paraphrase: nothing is done by our own doing; whatever happens, happens in His rang. Rang is the key word. It means color, and dye. But in Punjabi it also means joy, love, mood, the delight of a festival. So when Gurbani says everything happens in His rang, it's saying more than: God controls everything. It's saying everything is soaked in God, the way dyed cloth is soaked in color. Our actions are still ours, the way the cloth is still cloth. Sikhs work hard, study, serve, and plan; nobody is told to sit and wait. But every thread of that doing is already colored by the One we've called the Giver, the One full of every power. The strength in your arms, the idea that arrived, the breath that let you finish the sentence: none of it was manufactured from nothing by you alone. Gurbani's favorite version of this picture is a deep red dye from the madder root, majeeth. Cloth dyed with majeeth was said to keep its color through every wash. Many hymns ask to be dyed like that, so deeply in the Name that nothing washes it out. So nothing on our own isn't an insult to your effort. It's a description of what your effort is made of. And it leads straight to the practice: when the doing is soaked in someone else's color, the natural response, when it's done, is thanks.
screen: `THE DOER OF ALL, ANOTHER SIDE.` · `RANG: COLOR, DYE, JOY, LOVE.` · `STILL CLOTH, BUT SOAKED THROUGH.` · `MAJEETH: THE COLOR THAT STAYS.` · then, large: `IN HIS COLOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing and give thanks. Pick something tiny you can do right here: straighten your back, take one slow, full breath, unclench your hands. Do it with attention. Then notice what made it possible: the muscles, the air, the moment of quiet. Let a thank-you rise, to whoever or whatever you understand that to be. Do it again with the next small thing. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at each thank-you. The bell holds the time.
Nothing on our own. Everything happens in His rang, His color: our doing is still ours, like cloth, but soaked through, like dye.
Your line: in his color. Today, after you finish one piece of work, pause for a single breath and give thanks before you start the next. Day four hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Gurbani often speaks of being dyed in the Name, like cloth in fast madder dye, and Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's fifteenth ashtpadi hear that nothing is done by one's own doing alone.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rang, color or dye, and also joy, love or delight.

trapdoor: what you thought: nothing on our own means we're puppets.
what it means: our actions are ours, but soaked in God through every thread, so thanks comes naturally.
what a scholar hears: Gurbani contrasts majeeth, fast madder dye, with kusumbh, safflower, a bright dye that fades: lasting love against fleeting attachment.
